title: Bidirectional BFS in Barcelona: Cut the Search ⚡
description: Watch two BFS explorers launch at the same time—one from the start street, one from the destination—until they meet. This “meeting in the middle” technique dramatically reduces visited nodes and speeds up shortest-path routing.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — how two simultaneous searches doubles speed ⚡

Imagine Eixample blocks like a grid graph: each intersection is a node, streets are edges.

✅ Standard BFS expands outward from the start until it reaches the goal.
❗ The visited set can balloon because you’re exploring “one direction” only.

🚀 Bidirectional BFS does this instead:
1) BFS from START forward: distS, parentS
2) BFS from GOAL backward: distT, parentT
3) Expand the smaller frontier each step (common optimization)
4) Stop the moment frontiers intersect: node m
5) Reconstruct the path by stitching parent chains: parentS(m) + parentT(m)

📌 Takeaway: if the graph branching factor is b and shortest path length is d, single-source BFS explores ~b^d, but bidirectional BFS often explores ~2·b^(d/2). That’s the “cuts search space in half” vibe—fewer expansions, faster shortest paths.

🔥 Coding interview prep: implement queue pairs + visited maps (or parent maps) for both directions.

Debate question: Should you always expand alternately, or always expand the smaller frontier for best real-world performance?
